headline: Commercial shipping visible via http://MarineTraffic.com shows traffic transiting the Strait of Hormuz has slowed to a trickle over the past 24 hours, with just five merchant vessels completing the transit-all via the Iranian (northern) traffic separation scheme. One vessel, Jin Zeng 5, initially appeared to be routing through the U.S. established safe route through Omani waters, but altered course before entering the Strait and instead completed its transit through the Iranian channel. It is possible additional vessels transited the Strait with their Automatic Identification System (AIS) transponders disabled, in which case they would not appear in publicly available tracking data. Even so, the visible traffic suggests commercial operators continue to overwhelmingly favor the Iranian route despite the availability of the expanded southern corridor.

headline: RT by @sentdefender: The DoD's publicly released casualty totals for Operation EPIC FURY have been updated several times over the past three weeks, but the only recorded change since June 12 has been the addition of one non-hostile death. That stands in contrast to observable medical evacuation activity. During the same period, three C-17 medevac flights cycled through Joint Base Andrews after transporting patients from Germany, the Middle East, and Africa, each met by ambulance buses and/or patient evacuation vehicles for onward movement to Walter Reed National Military Medical Center. At least one patient was subsequently flown to Brooke Army Medical Center in San Antonio, TX, the Department of Defense's only Level I Trauma Center and verified Burn Center. While medical evacuations alone do not indicate changes in casualty totals, the continuation of flights meeting large medical transport vehicles who then return to Walter Reed with emergency lights activated indicates that the reported numbers may be an under count.

headline: The Joint Maritime Information Center (JMIC) has issued a new advisory stating that the expanded southern transit corridor through the Strait of Hormuz remains open and available to all commercial traffic, despite the recent series of attacks targeting vessels along the U.S.-supported route through Omani waters. headline: Commercial shipping visible transiting the Strait of Hormuz over the past 24 hours, via http://MarineTraffic.com, continues to overwhelmingly favor the Iranian (northern) traffic separation scheme, with approximately 10 completed merchant vessel transits. At least two of those vessels initially appeared to be routing toward the U.S.-supported southern corridor through Omani waters, but altered course before entering the Strait and instead crossed over to the Iranian traffic separation scheme. Overall, only one vessel was observed completing its transit via the Omani (southern) corridor. While additional vessels may be transiting with their Automatic Identification System (AIS) disabled and therefore not visible on publicly available tracking data, doing so would be contrary to current Joint Maritime Information Center (JMIC) guidance, which advises vessels to maintain AIS transmissions, radar, navigation lights, and continuous VHF radio monitoring while transiting the Strait.
